label: lem:GD
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:GD}
Let
$
Y_i
\in
\{1,\ldots,\ell\},
$
be latent variables satisfying
$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=r)
=
\pi_r,
\ 
r=1,\ldots,\ell.
$
Let
\[
T\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^m X_i,
\quad
V_i^*\coloneqq\frac{X_i}{T},
\quad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Then, 
conditional on
$
Y_1={j_1},
\ldots,
Y_m={j_m},
$
the random vector admits the stochastic representation
    
                       
                 
                         
    
\begin{align}\label{rep-est}
(X_1,\ldots,X_m)^\top
\stackrel{d}{=}
T(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top,
\end{align}
where
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)]  $
T\mid 
\left\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m
\right\}
\sim
\text{Gamma}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i},
\lambda
\right),
$
    \item[(b)] 
$
(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top\mid 
\left\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m
\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(
\alpha_{j_1},
\ldots,
\alpha_{j_m}
)
$, and
    \item[(c)] 
\(T\) and
\((V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top\)
being conditionally independent given
$Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m$.
\end{enumerate}

Moreover, if
$
S
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i,
$
then
\[
\left(
\frac{X_1}{S},
\ldots,
\frac{X_n}{S}
\right)^\top
\Bigg|
\left\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n
\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(
\alpha_{j_1},
\ldots,
\alpha_{j_n}
)
\]
and 
\(S\) and
\((X_1/S,\ldots,X_n/S)^\top\)
are conditionally independent given
$Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n$.
head: environment
name: Gamma--Dirichlet mixture representation

title: Proof
body_md:
Conditional on
$
Y_i=j_i,\  i=1,\ldots,m,
$
the random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ are independent, with
$
X_i\mid \{Y_i=j_i\}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha_{j_i},\lambda),
\ i=1,\ldots,m.
$
The classical Gamma--Dirichlet decomposition \citep{Devroye1986}
then implies that
\[
T
\mid 
\left\{Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i},\lambda
\right),
\]
and
\[
(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top
\mid 
\left\{Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m}),
\]
with $T$ and $(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top$ being conditionally independent given
$Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m$.

Consequently, using the identity
\[
(X_1,\ldots,X_m)^\top
=
T
(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top,
\]
we obtain the
stochastic representation in \eqref{rep-est}.

Applying the same argument to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, conditional on
$Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n$,
and letting $S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i$, we obtain
\[
S
\;\big|\;
\left\{Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{j_i},\lambda
\right),
\]
and
\[
\left(
\frac{X_1}{S},\ldots,\frac{X_n}{S}
\right)^\top
\Bigg|\,
\left\{Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_n}),
\]
with $S$ and the normalized vector $\left(
{X_1}/{S},\ldots,{X_n}/{S}
\right)^\top$ being conditionally independent  given
$Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n$.

label: prop:Ig
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the law of total expectation,
\[
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)]
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\mathbb{E}
\left(
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
\mid
Y_1,\ldots,Y_m
\right)
\right].
\]

Condition on
$
Y_1={j_1},
\ldots,
Y_m={j_m}.
$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:GD},
$
(X_1,\ldots,X_m)^\top
\stackrel{d}{=}
T(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top,
$
where
$$
T\mid 
\left\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m
\right\}
\sim
\text{Gamma}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i},
\lambda
\right),
$$
$$
(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top\mid 
\left\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m
\right\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(
\alpha_{j_1},
\ldots,
\alpha_{j_m}
),
$$
and \(T\) is conditionally independent of
\((V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)^\top\).

Since \(g\) is positively homogeneous of degree one,
$
g(TV_1^*,\ldots,TV_m^*)
=
Tg(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*),
$
and therefore, for $(V_1,\ldots,V_m)^\top
\sim \operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m})
$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}
\bigl[
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
&\mid
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m
\bigr]
\\[0,2cm]
&=
\mathbb{E}[T\mid
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m]
\,
\mathbb{E}
[g(V_1^*,\ldots,V_m^*)\mid
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m]
\\[0,2cm]
&=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i}
}
{\lambda}
\,
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m})}
[g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)],
\end{align*}
where, in the last equality, we used
$
\mathbb{E}[T\mid Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_m=j_m]
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i}
\right)/
\lambda.
$
Thus,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}
\left[
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
\mid
Y_1,\ldots,Y_m
\right]
=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{Y_i}
}
{\lambda}
\,
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{Y_1},\ldots,\alpha_{Y_m})}
[g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)].
\end{aligned}
\]

Taking expectation with respect to the latent variables $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ and applying the law of total expectation yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)]
=
\frac1{\lambda}
\sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_m=1}^{\ell}
\left(
\prod_{i=1}^{m}\pi_{j_i}
\right)
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j_i}
\right)
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m})}
[g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)].
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, since
$
\mu
=
({1}/{\lambda})\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\pi_r\alpha_r,
$
the stated representation follows immediately from the above equality
and the definition of $I(g)$.

label: thm:Expectation
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of $\widehat{I(g)}$ and the exchangeability of
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I(g)}]
=
\frac1{mC_g}\, 
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\frac{
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
}
{
\overline X
}
\right].
\]

Using
$
\overline X=S/n,
\
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i,
$
we obtain
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I(g)}]
=
\frac n{mC_g} 
\,
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\frac{
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
}
{
S
}
\right].
\]

By assumption (A1),
$
g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
=
S
g\left(
{X_1}/{S},
\ldots,
{X_m}/{S}
\right),
$
which immediately gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I(g)}]
=
\frac n{mC_g}
\,
\mathbb{E}
\left[
g
\left(
\frac{X_1}{S},
\ldots,
\frac{X_m}{S}
\right)
\right].
\]

Now,
Lemma~\ref{lem:GD} implies
$$
\left(
\frac{X_1}{S},
\ldots,
\frac{X_n}{S}
\right)^\top 
\Bigg|\,
\{
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n
\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(
\alpha_{j_1},
\ldots,
\alpha_{j_n}
),
$$
and therefore, for $(U_1,\ldots,U_n)^\top
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}
(
\alpha_{j_1},
\ldots,
\alpha_{j_n}
)$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}
\left[
g
\left(
\frac{X_1}{S},
\ldots,
\frac{X_m}{S}
\right)
\middle|
Y_1=j_1,\ldots,Y_n=j_n
\right]
&=
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_n})}
\!\left[
g(U_1,\ldots,U_m)
\right],
\\[0,2cm]
&=
{\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_{j_i}\over \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_{j_i}} 
\,
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}
(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m})}
\!\left[
g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)
\right],
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from the aggregation property of the
Dirichlet distribution. Specifically, with
$$
(V_1,\ldots,V_m)^\top 
\stackrel{d}{=}
\left(\frac{U_1}{\sum_{i=1}^m U_i},\ldots,\frac{U_m}{\sum_{i=1}^m U_i}\right)^\top
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}(\alpha_{j_1},\ldots,\alpha_{j_m}),
$$
independently of $\sum_{i=1}^m U_i$, and
$
\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i=1}^m U_i]
=
{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_{j_i}}/
{\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_{j_i}},
$
while $g$ is homogeneous of degree one.

                                                  
Applying the law of total expectation yields the desired identity, completing the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:Bias
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The bias in Corollary \ref{cor:Bias} admits the following decomposition:
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{I(g)},I(g))
&=\frac{1}{mC_g}
\Bigg\{
\mathbb{E}\Bigg[
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{Y_i}\right)
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}(\alpha_{Y_1},\ldots,\alpha_{Y_m})}
\left[g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)\right]
\Bigg]
\left(
n\mathbb{E}\left[
\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{Y_i}}
\right]
-\frac{1}{\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\pi_r\alpha_r}
\right)
\\[0,2cm]
&+
n\operatorname{Cov}\Bigg(
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{Y_i}\right)
\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{Dir}(\alpha_{Y_1},\ldots,\alpha_{Y_m})}
\left[g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)\right],
\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{Y_i}}
\Bigg)
\Bigg\}.
\end{align*}
Since the function $x\mapsto 1/x$ is convex on $(0,\infty)$, Jensen's inequality gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[
\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{Y_i}}
\right]
\geqslant
\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{Y_i}\right]}
=
\frac{1}{n\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\pi_r\alpha_r}.
\]
Hence,
\[
n\mathbb{E}\left[
\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{Y_i}}
\right]
-\frac{1}{\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\pi_r\alpha_r}
\geqslant 0.
\]
Moreover, since $g\geqslant 0$, the expectation multiplying this nonnegative quantity is also nonnegative. Therefore, the first contribution to the bias is nonnegative. The sign of the bias as a whole, however, depends on the covariance term. In particular, a nonnegative covariance guarantees a nonnegative bias, whereas a negative covariance does not necessarily imply a negative bias: it must be sufficiently negative to offset the first contribution. Thus, the sign of the bias cannot, in general, be determined solely from the nonnegativity of $g$ or from Jensen's inequality.
head: environment

label: cor:gamma
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:gamma}
Suppose that the finite Gamma mixture reduces to a single Gamma distribution, namely,
$
\ell=1,
\
X\sim\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda).
$
Then,
$
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I(g)}]=I(g),
\ 
n\geqslant m,
$
or, equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{I(g)},I(g))=0.
\]
Hence, the U-statistic estimator is exactly unbiased for every NSII generated by a nonnegative measurable symmetric function satisfying {\rm(A1)}--{\rm(A2)}.

label: thm:asymptotic-normality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:asymptotic-normality}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:Expectation},
\[
\sqrt{n}
\left\{
\widehat{I(g)}-I(g)
\right\}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{D}}
N
\left(
0,\frac{\sigma_g^2}{C_g^2\mu^2}
+
\frac{\theta_g^2\sigma_X^2}
{m^2C_g^2\mu^4}
-
\frac{2\theta_g\tau_g}
{mC_g^2\mu^3}
\right),
\quad n\to\infty,
\]
where $\xrightarrow{\mathscr{D}}
$ denotes convergence in distribution,
$
\theta_g
=
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)],
\ 
\sigma_g^2
=
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\mid X_1]
\right),
\ 
\tau_g
=
\operatorname{Cov}
\left(
\mathbb{E}[g(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\mid X_1],
X_1
\right),
$
and
$
\sigma_X^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1).
$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By (A2),
$
0\leqslant g(x_1,\ldots,x_m)
\leqslant C_g\sum_{i=1}^m x_i.
$
Since the finite Gamma mixture has finite moments of all orders,
$
\mathbb{E}[g^2(X_1,\ldots,X_m)]<\infty.
$
Hence, the asymptotic normality of $U$-statistics \citep[Theorem 7.3 of][]{Hoeffding1948} yields
\[
\sqrt{n}
\left\{
U_n(g)-\theta_g
\right\}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{D}}
N(0,m^2\sigma_g^2),
\quad n\to\infty,
\]
where $U_n(g)$ is as defined in \eqref{eq:Us}.
Moreover, the multivariate central limit theorem gives the joint
convergence
\[
\sqrt{n}
\begin{pmatrix}
U_n(g)-\theta_g
\\[0,2cm]
\overline X-\mu
\end{pmatrix}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{D}}
N_2(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}),
\quad 
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
m^2\sigma_g^2&m\tau_g
\\[0,2cm]
m\tau_g&\sigma_X^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Consider
$
h(u,v)={u}/({mC_gv}).
$
Since $\mu>0$, $h$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of
$(\theta_g,\mu)^\top$, with gradient
$
\nabla h(\theta_g,\mu)
=
(
{1}/({mC_g\mu}),
-{\theta_g}/({mC_g\mu^2})
)^{\!\top}.
$
Therefore, by the multivariate delta method,
\[
\sqrt{n}
\left\{
h(U_n(g),\overline{X})-h(\theta_g,\mu)
\right\}
\stackrel{\eqref{eq:Tn}}{=}
\sqrt{n}
\left\{
\widehat{I(g)}-I(g)
\right\}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{D}}
N(0,\sigma_I^2),
\quad 
n\to\infty,
\]
where
$
\sigma_I^2
=
[\nabla h(\theta_g,\mu)]^\top
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\nabla h(\theta_g,\mu).
   
                               
   
                             
                 
   
                        
                
$

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of $\widehat{I(g)}$ and assumption (A1),
\[
\widehat{I(g)}
=
\frac{n}
{mC_g\binom{n}{m}}
\sum_{A\in\mathcal A_{n,m}}g(U_A),
\]
where
$
\mathcal A_{n,m}
=
\{A\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}:|A|=m\}.
$
Hence,
\[
\mathbb E[\widehat{I(g)}^2]
=
\frac{n^2}
{m^2C_g^2\binom{n}{m}^2}
\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal A_{n,m}}
\mathbb E[g(U_A)g(U_B)].
\]

For a fixed $A$, the number of subsets $B$ satisfying
$|A\cap B|=q$ is
$
\binom{m}{q}\binom{n-m}{m-q}.
$
By the exchangeability of $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ and the symmetry of $g$,
the corresponding expectation depends on $(A,B)^\top$ only through
$q=|A\cap B|$. Thus, we may take
$
A=\{1,\ldots,m\},
\
B=\{1,\ldots,q,m+1,\ldots,2m-q\},
$
which gives $H_q$. Summing over $q$ yields the result.

body_md:
\label{cor:variance-gamma}
Consider the special case in which the finite Gamma mixture consists of
a single Gamma distribution, namely,
$
\ell=1,
\ 
X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda).
$
Then,
{\small
\begin{align*}
\!\!\!\!\!
&\operatorname{Var}[\widehat{I(g)}]
=
\frac{n}
{m^2(n\alpha+1) C_g^2 \binom{n}{m}}
\sum_{q=q_0}^{m}
\binom{m}{q}
\binom{n-m}{m-q}
\\[0,2cm]
&\times 
\Bigg\{
d_q(d_q\alpha+1)
\mathbb E_{\operatorname{Dir}_{d_q}(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)}
\Big[
g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)
g(V_1,\ldots,V_q,V_{m+1},\ldots,V_{d_q})
\Big]
-
\frac{m^2(n\alpha+1)}{n}
\left\{
\mathbb E_{\operatorname{Dir}_m(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)}
\left[
g(V_1,\ldots,V_m)
\right]
\right\}^{2}
\Bigg\},
\end{align*}
}\noindent
where
$
(V_1,\ldots,V_m)^\top 
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}_m
(
\alpha,
\ldots,
\alpha
)
$,
$
(V_1,\ldots,V_{d_q})^\top
\sim
\operatorname{Dir}_{d_q}(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha)
$
$q_0=\max\{0,2m-n\}$ and $d_q=2m-q$.

Consequently,
$
\operatorname{MSE}[\widehat{I(g)}]
=
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat{I(g)}].
$
